gloss_terse: to bristle up, to stand on end (of hair or flesh from fear or dread)
gloss_readable: This verb captures the visceral physical reaction when fear grips the body—hair standing on end, flesh 'creeping' with dread. The Hebrew is rare, appearing only twice, but both contexts involve an encounter with God's terrifying majesty. In Psalm 119:120, the psalmist confesses that his very flesh bristles from fear of God, while in Job 4:15, Eliphaz describes a spirit passing before his face, making the hair of his flesh stand up in terror.

senses.1: Used in both occurrences to describe the physical response of hair or flesh standing erect due to overwhelming fear or dread, particularly in contexts of divine encounter. The Spanish 'se-erizó' (stood on end) and English 'made-stand-up' capture the involuntary bodily reaction, while 'trembles' reflects the emotional state. Job 4:15 depicts a supernatural encounter, while Psalm 119:120 expresses reverent fear before God's commands.

gloss_terse: Senuah (personal name); father or ancestor of Judahite leaders in post-exilic Jerusalem
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in genealogies of post-exilic Jerusalem, specifically in lists of those who resettled the city after the Babylonian captivity. The name occurs with the definite article (ha-Senuah) in both passages, suggesting it may be a clan or family designation. 1 Chronicles 9:7 and Nehemiah 11:9 record Judahite leaders whose lineage traced through 'the son of ha-Senuah,' indicating this was a recognized family line in the restored community.

senses.1: A proper name in genealogical lists, appearing as 'ha-Senuah' (with the article) in both occurrences. The parallel passages in Chronicles and Nehemiah identify this as an ancestral name in the lineage of post-exilic Judahite leaders. Greek versions transliterate it variously as Asana, Asenna, Aana, suggesting uncertainty about the original pronunciation.

gloss_terse: Sismai (personal name); descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel
gloss_readable: This name appears in the genealogy of Judah, specifically within the extensive family tree of Jerahmeel recorded in 1 Chronicles 2. The name occurs twice in the same verse with slight spelling variation in the Masoretic text (Sismai and Sismai), though this likely reflects scribal variation rather than different individuals. The genealogical context places Sismai within the southern tribes, preserving the memory of Judahite clans from the pre-exilic period.

senses.1: A personal name in the genealogical records of Judah's tribe, specifically within Jerahmeel's lineage. Both occurrences are in 1 Chronicles 2:40, with the conjunction 'and' marking the continuation of the genealogy. The Greek versions (Sosomai, Sasamei) attempt to preserve the Hebrew phonetics.

gloss_terse: disquieting thoughts, troubled thoughts, anxious mental agitation
gloss_readable: This plural noun describes the kind of thoughts that disturb sleep and peace—racing, anxious, disquieting reflections that agitate the mind. Both occurrences are in Job's dialogues, where intense suffering provokes mental anguish. In Job 4:13, Eliphaz speaks of troubled thoughts during visions of the night, while in Job 20:2, Zophar's 'disquieting thoughts' compel him to respond hastily to Job. The word captures mental restlessness and inner turmoil.

senses.1: Describes agitated, troubled, or disquieting thoughts that disturb mental peace. The contexts in Job link these thoughts to suffering, visions, and urgent compulsion to speak. Spanish 'pensamientos' and French references to troubled thoughts align with the Hebrew sense of mental agitation. In Job 20:2, parallel with 'my haste within me' intensifies the image of inner turmoil.

gloss_terse: boughs, branches (of a tree, especially cedar)
gloss_readable: This feminine plural noun refers to the spreading branches or boughs of a great tree. Both occurrences are in Ezekiel 31, where Assyria is depicted as a magnificent cedar in Lebanon, so tall and majestic that birds nest in its boughs and nations find shelter under its branches. The imagery emphasizes grandeur and protective reach—the sprawling canopy of a mighty tree. The prophet uses this arboreal metaphor to describe imperial power before announcing its impending fall.

senses.1: The branches or boughs of a great tree, used metaphorically in Ezekiel 31 for the far-reaching power of Assyria. Both references (vv. 6, 8) speak of birds nesting and nations dwelling 'in its boughs,' highlighting the protective and expansive nature of the cedar's canopy. The Hebrew occurs with possessive suffix 'its boughs,' emphasizing the majestic cedar figure.

gloss_terse: storm, whirlwind, tempest
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a violent storm or whirlwind, the kind of atmospheric fury that announces divine presence. Both occurrences in Job describe God speaking to Job 'out of the storm'—a theophanic manifestation where the Creator addresses His creature from the heart of nature's power. The storm is not merely meteorological but theological, a fitting medium for the overwhelming majesty of God's voice. The tempest symbolizes both terror and revelation.

senses.1: A fierce storm or whirlwind, specifically the tempest from which YHWH speaks to Job (38:1, 40:6). The repetition emphasizes this as the signature setting for God's climactic self-revelation. Cross-linguistic glosses consistently render this as 'storm' or 'tempest,' recognizing the theophanic context where divine speech emerges from natural fury.

gloss_terse: scab, eruption (skin lesion or disease)
gloss_readable: This noun refers to a skin eruption, scab, or lesion—a dermatological condition examined in Levitical purity laws. The word appears in lists of skin afflictions that priests must diagnose to determine ritual cleanness or uncleanness. Leviticus 13:2 groups it with swelling and bright spot, while 14:56 includes it in the summary of conditions addressed in the purification ritual. The term is clinical and priestly, part of ancient Israel's health and holiness code.

senses.1: A skin condition—scab or eruption—examined in priestly diagnosis of ritual purity (Leviticus 13-14). Both occurrences appear in formulaic lists alongside other skin lesions. The multilingual glosses (Spanish 'erupción,' German 'Schorf,' French 'croûte') all identify this as a dermatological abnormality requiring priestly evaluation for ritual status.

gloss_terse: bowl, basin (large vessel for liquids)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a large bowl or basin, likely for holding liquids. The two biblical occurrences capture different nuances: in Judges 5:25, Jael offers Sisera milk 'in a bowl of nobles'—a magnificent vessel befitting royalty, underscoring the ironic hospitality before his death. In Judges 6:38, Gideon wrings out the fleece and fills 'the bowl' with dew, demonstrating God's sign. The word suggests a substantial, possibly ornate vessel, distinguished from everyday containers.

senses.1: A substantial bowl or basin for holding liquids. In Judges 5:25, it's a 'bowl of nobles,' suggesting size and quality; in 6:38, it holds the dew wrung from the fleece. Cross-linguistic renderings (Spanish 'tazón,' French 'bol,' German 'bowl') all point to a sizable container, though the etymology remains uncertain—possibly a foreign loanword.

gloss_terse: Sophereth (personal name); ancestor of returned exiles, temple servants
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a family line among the returned exiles, specifically among 'the sons of the servants of Solomon'—a group of temple servants who traced their lineage to Solomon's administrative staff. The name appears in parallel lists: Ezra 2:55 and Nehemiah 7:57, both cataloging families who returned from Babylonian captivity to resettle Jerusalem. The slight spelling variation (ha-Soferet vs. Sophereth) reflects the same family group, preserving their claim to service in the restored temple community.

senses.1: A proper name designating a family of temple servants among the post-exilic returnees. Both occurrences are in genealogical lists ('sons of Sophereth'), indicating this was a recognized clan within the larger group of 'Solomon's servants.' The presence in both Ezra and Nehemiah's parallel lists confirms their place in the restored community.

gloss_terse: mantle, cloak, tunic (outer garment)
gloss_readable: This noun refers to an outer garment—possibly a mantle, cloak, or tunic—though the exact nature of the garment is debated. Both occurrences are in Daniel 3, where Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are thrown into the fiery furnace 'in their cloaks' along with their other garments. The word is likely a Persian loanword, reflecting the Babylonian setting. The miracle is heightened by noting they were bound in full dress yet emerged unsinged, without even the smell of fire on their garments.

senses.1: An outer garment worn by the three young men in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3:21, 27). The context emphasizes they were cast in 'bound in their cloaks' (v. 21) and emerged with garments unharmed (v. 27). Cross-linguistic glosses suggest 'cloak' or 'tunic,' though 'trousers' is also proposed. The term is likely borrowed from Persian.

gloss_terse: Sered (personal name); son of Zebulun, ancestor of the Sardites
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies one of the three sons of Zebulun listed in Genesis 46:14, among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Numbers 26:26 confirms Sered as the ancestor of the Sardite clan, one of the Zebulunite families enumerated in the wilderness census. The name thus marks both an individual patriarch and the clan that descended from him, preserving tribal memory through genealogical record.

senses.1: A proper name for Zebulun's son and the ancestral head of the Sardite clan. Genesis 46:14 lists him among Jacob's descendants who migrated to Egypt; Numbers 26:26 traces the Sardite family back to 'Sered.' The cross-linguistic glosses uniformly preserve the name, with grammatical variations ('to Sered,' 'of Sered') reflecting case relationships.

gloss_terse: armor, coat of mail (protective body covering for battle)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes defensive armor, specifically a coat of mail or breastplate worn in battle. Both occurrences are in Jeremiah's oracles against Babylon and Egypt, military contexts where warriors prepare for combat. In Jeremiah 46:4, soldiers are commanded to 'put on the armor' alongside other battle preparations. In 51:3, warriors are to 'raise themselves in their armor' against Babylon. The word is a variant form of the more common shiryon, emphasizing military readiness and protection.

senses.1: Protective armor or coat of mail worn by soldiers in battle. The contexts in Jeremiah involve military mobilization: donning armor (46:4) and standing ready in armor (51:3). Cross-linguistic glosses uniformly render this as 'armor' or 'breastplate,' recognizing the military context of divine judgment enacted through warfare.

gloss_terse: winter (cold/rainy season)
gloss_readable: This noun refers to the winter season—the time of cold and rain in the land. The single biblical context is Song of Solomon 2:11, where the beloved declares 'the winter is past, the rain is over and gone,' signaling spring's arrival and the renewal of love. The word is a loanword from Aramaic, reflecting linguistic interchange. Winter represents dormancy and waiting, while its passing brings joy, growth, and the lover's reunion.

senses.1: The winter season, characterized by cold and rain. Song of Solomon 2:11 celebrates winter's departure as a sign of spring and renewal. The Hebrew shows ketiv/qere variation (setaw/setayv), reflecting scribal traditions. Cross-linguistic glosses consistently identify this as 'winter,' with the Aramaic loanword indicating linguistic borrowing.

gloss_terse: Abda (personal name); father of Adoniram (Solomon's official) and a Levite
gloss_readable: This personal name means 'servant' or 'servant of Yahweh,' similar in meaning to Obadiah. It identifies two individuals: first, the father of Adoniram, Solomon's official in charge of forced labor (1 Kings 4:6); second, a Levite listed among those resettled in post-exilic Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:17). The name reflects piety and dedication, common in Israelite naming conventions where theophoric elements express devotion to God.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in two contexts: (1) father of Adoniram, Solomon's labor minister (1 Kings 4:6), and (2) a post-exilic Levite (Nehemiah 11:17). The name means 'servant (of Yahweh),' parallel to Obadiah. Greek versions show uncertainty (Ephra, Abaō, Ōbēb), but the Hebrew is consistent across both occurrences.

gloss_terse: household servants, body of servants (collective)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes a household's body of servants collectively—not individual slaves but the entire service staff as a group. Both occurrences list 'servants' alongside flocks, herds, and other wealth indicators. Genesis 26:14 describes Isaac's prosperity: 'flocks and herds and a great household of servants,' while Job 1:3 similarly catalogs Job's wealth including 'very many servants.' The word emphasizes the household as an economic and social unit, with servants representing labor capacity and status.

senses.1: The collective body of household servants, listed among wealth indicators alongside livestock and possessions. Genesis 26:14 and Job 1:3 both enumerate servants as part of patriarchal prosperity. Spanish 'servidumbre' (household staff) and German 'Gesinde' (servants collectively) capture the collective sense better than individual 'servants.'

gloss_terse: Abednego (personal name); Babylonian name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three companions
gloss_readable: This is the Babylonian throne name given to Azariah, one of Daniel's three faithful companions in exile. The name appears to be a deliberate or accidental corruption of 'Abed-Nebo' (servant of Nebo, the Babylonian deity), possibly altered to avoid pronouncing a pagan god's name fully. Both occurrences in Daniel 1:7 record the renaming of the Hebrew youths: Azariah becomes Abednego. The name symbolizes Babylonian cultural imposition, yet Azariah and his friends maintain covenant faithfulness despite foreign names.

senses.1: The Babylonian name assigned to Azariah, Daniel's companion, recorded twice in Daniel 1:7 during the renaming ceremony. The name likely means 'servant of Nebo' but may be intentionally corrupted from the pagan theophoric element. The dual reference emphasizes both the Hebrew identity (Azariah) and imposed Babylonian identity (Abednego).

gloss_terse: produce, yield (of the land)
gloss_readable: This noun refers to agricultural produce or yield—the crops and food that the land produces. Both occurrences are in Joshua 5:11-12, marking Israel's first Passover in Canaan. After eating 'the produce of the land,' the manna ceased—a pivotal moment when wilderness provision ended and agricultural settlement began. The word emphasizes the land's fertility and God's provision through natural means rather than supernatural miracle, transitioning Israel from nomadic to agricultural life.

senses.1: The agricultural produce or yield of the land, specifically the crops of Canaan eaten by Israel after entering the promised land (Joshua 5:11-12). The context marks the transition from manna to cultivated food, from wilderness to settlement. Cross-linguistic glosses render this as 'produce' or 'yield,' emphasizing the land's output.

gloss_terse: to pass through, transgress (in these contexts)
gloss_readable: While this common verb typically means 'to pass over' or 'pass through,' these two occurrences carry connotations of transgression or spiritual unfaithfulness. In Jeremiah 2:20, God accuses Israel of breaking the yoke and transgressing covenant; in Nahum 1:15, the promise that 'the wicked one will no more pass through you' suggests enemy invasion or spiritual violation. Both contexts involve boundary-crossing in a negative sense—rebellion or hostile intrusion.

senses.1: Used in these contexts with overtones of transgression or violation. Jeremiah 2:20 speaks of covenant-breaking ('I will transgress'), while Nahum 1:15 promises cessation of enemy incursion ('no more pass through you'). Though the basic meaning is 'pass through,' the contexts emphasize illicit crossing of boundaries—moral, covenantal, or territorial.

gloss_terse: ford (river crossing place)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes a ford—a shallow place in a river where people and animals can cross on foot. The two occurrences in 2 Samuel involve David's flight from Absalom. In 15:28 (with textual variant), David waits 'at the fords of the wilderness' for word from Jerusalem; in 19:18, they cross 'the ford' to bring the king back. Fords were strategic locations for travel and communication, especially in times of political crisis when bridges might be controlled or destroyed.

senses.1: A river ford or crossing place. Both references in 2 Samuel relate to crossing the Jordan during David's flight from and return after Absalom's rebellion. The Hebrew shows textual variants (ketiv/qere) between 'fords' and 'plains,' but 'fords' fits the context of river crossing. Such locations were militarily and logistically significant.

gloss_terse: Abronah (place name); wilderness encampment of Israel, one station from Ezion-geber
gloss_readable: This place name identifies one of Israel's encampments during the wilderness wandering, located one march from Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba. Numbers 33:34-35 records the itinerary: they departed from Ezion-geber and camped at Abronah, then departed from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber. The location is uncertain, somewhere in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, marking Israel's progress toward Canaan along the eastern trade routes.

senses.1: A place name marking an Israelite encampment in the wilderness wandering (Numbers 33:34-35). The site lay along the route from Ezion-geber, though exact location is unknown. Cross-linguistic glosses preserve the name with prepositional variations ('in Abronah,' 'from Abronah') reflecting Hebrew case relationships in the itinerary.

gloss_terse: sensuous love, lustful words or desires (plural intensive)
gloss_readable: This plural noun conveys sensuous or lustful love—desire with overtones of impropriety or insincerity. The sole clear occurrence is Ezekiel 33:32, where God tells Ezekiel, 'You are to them like a love song,' meaning the people enjoy his words aesthetically but don't obey them. The intensive plural suggests passionate but shallow affection. Some manuscripts include another occurrence in verse 31, though this is textually disputed. The word captures the danger of religious entertainment replacing genuine devotion.

senses.1: Sensuous or lustful love, used metaphorically in Ezekiel 33:32 to describe Israel's superficial attraction to prophetic words without commitment to obey. The 'love song' comparison suggests aesthetic pleasure divorced from moral response. The plural form intensifies the sense of passionate but ultimately empty affection. Spanish 'amores' and 'lisonjas' (flatteries) capture the insincere dimension.

gloss_terse: crane or swallow (bird, exact species uncertain)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a bird, likely a crane or swallow, though the exact species is debated. Isaiah 38:14 uses it alongside 'swallow' to describe Hezekiah's groaning in illness ('like a swallow or crane'), while Jeremiah 8:7 lists it among migratory birds that 'know their appointed times'—a rebuke to Israel who don't know God's ordinances. The bird's mournful cry or seasonal instinct provides prophetic imagery. Textual and etymological uncertainties persist, but the bird clearly represents either lamentation or natural obedience.

senses.1: A bird species, traditionally identified as crane or swallow. Isaiah 38:14 focuses on its cry (expressing pain); Jeremiah 8:7 emphasizes its migratory instinct (knowing divine timing). Cross-linguistic glosses settle on 'crane' or 'swallow,' though Hebrew etymology is uncertain. The bird serves as metaphor for human suffering and obedience to natural law.

gloss_terse: ring, earring, hoop (ornament worn on ear or body)
gloss_readable: This noun refers to a ring or hoop, typically an earring worn as adornment. Numbers 31:50 lists it among gold jewelry offered as tribute, alongside bracelets and chains. Ezekiel 16:12 describes God adorning personified Jerusalem with 'earrings on your ears' plus a nose ring, symbolizing covenant love and royal beautification. The word emphasizes personal ornamentation and wealth, often with covenantal or religious significance when jewelry is dedicated to God or received as divine gift.

senses.1: A ring or hoop, specifically earrings in both occurrences. Numbers 31:50 includes them in spoils of war dedicated to YHWH; Ezekiel 16:12 uses them metaphorically for God's covenant adornment of Israel. Spanish 'pendiente' and cross-linguistic 'earring' confirm the ornamental function, with religious and symbolic dimensions in covenant contexts.

gloss_terse: Eglath (place name); location in Moab, possibly 'third Eglath' or 'three-year-old heifer'
gloss_readable: This place name appears in prophetic oracles against Moab, with the enigmatic phrase 'Eglath Shelishiyah' (literally 'third Eglath' or possibly 'Eglath of the three-year-old heifer'). Isaiah 15:5 and Jeremiah 48:34 locate it near Zoar on Moab's southern border. The exact meaning and location are disputed—it may be a place name modified by 'third' or an image of a heifer. The Septuagint translates as 'three-year-old heifer,' suggesting the phrase may be metaphorical rather than purely geographical.

senses.1: A place name in Moab, appearing in the phrase 'Eglath Shelishiyah' (Isaiah 15:5; Jeremiah 48:34). The second element means 'third' or 'three-year-old,' leading to interpretations as either 'third Eglath' (implying multiple towns of that name) or 'heifer of three years' (metaphor). Located near Zoar, it marks Moab's southern territory in judgment oracles.

gloss_terse: Eglah (personal name); wife of David, mother of Ithream
gloss_readable: This personal name means 'heifer' and identifies one of David's wives during his reign in Hebron. Both occurrences—2 Samuel 3:5 and 1 Chronicles 3:3—list her as the mother of Ithream, David's sixth son. The name Eglah joins other pastoral names like Leah ('cow') and Rachel ('ewe'), reflecting ancient naming conventions that drew from animal imagery. She appears last in the list of Hebron wives, suggesting she may have been David's final wife before moving the capital to Jerusalem.

senses.1: A proper name for one of David's wives, mother of Ithream. The name means 'heifer,' fitting the pattern of pastoral names among biblical women (Leah, Rachel). Both references appear in parallel genealogical lists of David's sons born in Hebron. The name is consistently preserved across versions, with minor transliteration variants.

gloss_terse: to pass on, advance, remove (proceed forward or take away)
gloss_readable: This verb means to pass by, advance, or move forward—sometimes with the sense of removing something. In Job 28:8, the proud beasts have not 'advanced upon' the hidden path to wisdom, emphasizing wisdom's inaccessibility. Proverbs 25:20 speaks of 'removing a garment' on a cold day as a metaphor for inappropriate cheerfulness to a suffering person. The verb captures forward motion or the act of taking something away, with contexts determining whether emphasis falls on progression or removal.

senses.1: To pass on, advance, or remove. Job 28:8 uses it for advancing or passing over (the lion has not 'advanced upon' wisdom's path), while Proverbs 25:20 employs it for removing a garment. The semantic range spans motion forward and action of taking away. Cross-linguistic glosses show both senses: 'passed' and 'one who removes.'

gloss_terse: still, yet, hitherto (temporal adverb indicating continuance up to present)
gloss_readable: This adverb means 'still,' 'yet,' or 'hitherto'—a temporal marker indicating something continues up to the present moment or hasn't happened yet. Both occurrences are in Ecclesiastes 4, where Qohelet reflects on the superiority of the dead and unborn. Verse 2 praises those 'already dead' over the living, while verse 3 declares those 'not yet born' most fortunate. The adverb marks temporal boundaries in Qohelet's pessimistic assessment of life under the sun, contrasting past, present, and未-yet-realized states.

senses.1: A temporal adverb meaning 'still,' 'yet,' or 'hitherto.' Ecclesiastes 4:2 uses it for those 'already/still dead,' while 4:3 applies it to those 'yet/not yet born.' Cross-linguistic glosses (Spanish 'aún,' 'todavía'; English 'still,' 'yet') confirm the temporal continuance sense. The word derives from 'ad (until) + hennah (here), thus 'until now.'

gloss_terse: delight, pleasure (especially sensual/sexual)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes delight or pleasure, particularly with sensual or sexual overtones. Genesis 18:12 records Sarah's incredulous inward laugh: shall I have 'pleasure' (conjugal relations and childbearing) when I am old? Amos 1:5 mentions 'Beth-eden' (house of delight/pleasure), a location associated with Damascus. The word shares consonants with 'Eden,' the garden of delight, and carries connotations of enjoyment, luxury, and physical pleasure.

senses.1: Delight or pleasure with sensual overtones. Genesis 18:12 uses it for Sarah's anticipated pleasure in childbearing/conjugal relations despite old age. Amos 1:5 references 'Beth-eden' (possibly a place name meaning 'house of delight'). German 'Wonne' (bliss/delight) and Spanish 'placer' capture the pleasurable sense, which can be physical/sexual or more general enjoyment.

gloss_terse: Eden (personal name); Levite who served during Hezekiah's reforms
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a Levite active during Hezekiah's religious reforms. 2 Chronicles 29:12 lists Eden among Levites who sanctified themselves to cleanse the temple, while 31:15 names him as one who faithfully distributed offerings in the priestly cities. The name means 'delight' or 'pleasure,' sharing consonants with the garden of Eden. The Levite Eden represents faithful service during a time of covenant renewal and temple restoration.

senses.1: A proper name for a Levite during Hezekiah's reign, mentioned in temple cleansing (2 Chronicles 29:12) and distribution of offerings (31:15). The name means 'delight,' etymologically related to the garden of Eden. Greek versions (Iōadan, Odom, Iadan) show uncertainty in transliteration, but the Hebrew is consistent across both occurrences.

gloss_terse: Adna (personal name); identifies two post-exilic men
gloss_readable: This personal name appears in two post-exilic contexts, identifying different individuals. Ezra 10:30 lists Adna among those who had married foreign wives during the exile and were required to divorce them. Nehemiah 12:15 names an Adna as head of a priestly family in the generation after the return. The name likely means 'delight' or 'pleasure,' from the same root as Eden. Both occurrences reflect the reconstituted community's attention to genealogical and covenantal purity.

senses.1: A proper name for two post-exilic individuals: (1) a man who married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:30), and (2) a priestly family head (Nehemiah 12:15). The name means 'delight' or 'pleasure.' Cross-linguistic glosses preserve the name consistently, with Greek versions attempting transliteration (Aidaine, Edna, Adanas).

gloss_terse: Adnah (personal name); identifies a Judahite prince and a Manassite warrior
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies two military figures in Chronicles. 2 Chronicles 17:14 lists Adnah as a commander of Judah under Jehoshaphat, leading 300,000 mighty warriors. 1 Chronicles 12:21 names Adnah among the Manassite warriors who defected to David at Ziklag, becoming chiefs in his army. The name means 'delight' or 'pleasure,' likely theophoric. Both men exemplify military leadership and courage in supporting godly kings.

senses.1: A proper name for two military leaders: (1) a Manassite who joined David (1 Chronicles 12:21), and (2) a Judahite commander under Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 17:14). The name means 'delight,' related to Eden. Textual variants exist (Adnah/Adnach), and Greek versions show transliteration uncertainty (Edna, Adnas).

gloss_terse: to be hoed, to hoe (cultivate with a hoe or mattock)
gloss_readable: This verb in the Niphal (passive) stem refers to the agricultural practice of hoeing—breaking up soil with a hoe or mattock for cultivation. Both occurrences are in Isaiah's vineyard oracles. Isaiah 5:6 threatens that the rebellious vineyard 'will not be hoed' (nor pruned), allowing it to go wild. Isaiah 7:25 describes hills 'which used to be hoed with the hoe,' now abandoned to thorns due to invasion. The imagery emphasizes agricultural care and its absence as divine judgment.

senses.1: To be hoed or cultivated with a hoe/mattock, used passively in both occurrences. Isaiah 5:6 threatens cessation of hoeing as judgment on Israel-the-vineyard, while 7:25 speaks of hills formerly hoed now overrun by briers. The contexts link agricultural care to covenant blessing, and neglect to judgment. Cross-linguistic glosses render this as 'hoed' or 'cultivated.'

gloss_terse: Eder (personal name); Levite in the genealogy of Merari
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a Levite of the Merarite clan in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles. Both occurrences (23:23 and 24:30) place Eder within the descendants of Mushi, son of Merari. The name means 'flock' or 'herd,' common in Hebrew nomenclature. The parallel references confirm Eder's place in the Levitical structure, preserving tribal memory and organizational roles for temple service.

senses.1: A proper name for a Levite of Merari's line, appearing in parallel genealogical lists (1 Chronicles 23:23, 24:30). The name means 'flock,' fitting pastoral naming patterns. Both occurrences include the conjunction 'and Eder,' marking him in a series of Levitical descendants. Greek versions show transliteration variants (Aidath, Ēla, Eder).

gloss_terse: Adriel (personal name); son-in-law of Saul, married to Merab
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies Saul's son-in-law, who married Merab, Saul's daughter originally promised to David. 1 Samuel 18:19 records Merab being given to Adriel the Meholathite instead of David. 2 Samuel 21:8 mentions Adriel again in the tragic narrative of Saul's descendants being executed to end a famine. The name likely means 'my help is God' (an Aramaic equivalent to Hebrew Azriel), suggesting Aramaic cultural connections. Adriel's marriage and his sons' deaths reflect the political and covenantal complexities of Saul's reign.

senses.1: A proper name for Saul's son-in-law who married Merab (1 Samuel 18:19; 2 Samuel 21:8). The name means 'my help is God,' with Aramaic linguistic features. Both occurrences mark pivotal moments: the broken marriage promise to David and the execution of Adriel's sons. Cross-linguistic glosses preserve the name with appropriate prepositions.

gloss_terse: Avvim, Avvites (gentlic/ethnic designation); people group in Canaan/Syria
gloss_readable: This gentlic adjective (used as a substantive) designates an ethnic group, the Avvites. Joshua 13:3 lists them among Canaanite peoples in Philistine territory whom Israel did not dispossess. 2 Kings 17:31 identifies Avvites among the foreign groups resettled in Samaria by Assyria, who brought their gods (Nibhaz and Tartak) with them. The term marks a distinct people group, though their exact identity and origins remain somewhat obscure. They represent the incomplete conquest and later syncretistic threats to Israel's covenant purity.

senses.1: A gentlic designation for the Avvites, a people group mentioned in conquest (Joshua 13:3) and Assyrian resettlement contexts (2 Kings 17:31). Both occurrences include the definite article ('the Avvites'), identifying them as a recognized ethnic entity. Cross-linguistic glosses preserve the ethnic name with appropriate articles.

gloss_terse: young boys, little children (masculine plural)
gloss_readable: This masculine plural noun refers to young boys or small children, likely pre-adolescent. Both occurrences are in Job, where social relationships have inverted painfully. Job 19:18 laments that 'even young children despise me,' marking his social humiliation. Job 21:11 describes the prosperity of the wicked, whose 'little ones' go forth dancing. The word emphasizes youth and vulnerability, making the contexts more poignant—either mocking an outcast elder or symbolizing blessing and joy in family life.

senses.1: Young boys or small children, used in Job to depict social reversal (19:18) and familial blessing (21:11). Job 19:18 shows children mocking the sufferer—an inversion of respect. Job 21:11 portrays the wicked's children playing freely—a sign of prosperity. The term emphasizes childhood and the social meanings attached to children's treatment of adults.

gloss_terse: Avvim (place and people name); coastal people and a Benjamite city
gloss_readable: This name appears in two distinct contexts. Deuteronomy 2:23 describes the Avvim as a people living in villages near Gaza, destroyed by the Caphtorim (Philistines) who displaced them—a note on pre-Israelite population changes. Joshua 18:23 lists Avvim as a city in Benjamin's tribal allotment, possibly the same ethnic group settled as a town or a different location with similar name. The dual usage (ethnic and geographic) reflects the fluidity of ancient Near Eastern peoples and places.

senses.1: A name with both ethnic and geographic reference: (1) a people group near the Mediterranean coast displaced by Philistines (Deuteronomy 2:23), and (2) a Benjamite city (Joshua 18:23). Both occurrences use the definite article ('the Avvim'). The relationship between the coastal people and the Benjamite town is uncertain.

gloss_terse: to act unjustly, to deal wrongfully (Piel intensive)
gloss_readable: This verb in the Piel (intensive) stem means to act with injustice or perversity—to deal wrongfully, oppressively. Isaiah 26:10 warns that even when the wicked receive favor, 'he acts unjustly' and does not learn righteousness. Psalm 71:4 prays for deliverance from 'the hand of the unjust,' parallel to 'the wicked' and 'the ruthless.' The Piel formation intensifies the moral failure, emphasizing willful, persistent wrongdoing rather than accidental error.

senses.1: To act unjustly or deal wrongfully (Piel stem). Isaiah 26:10 describes the wicked who persist in injustice despite divine favor, while Psalm 71:4 names 'the unjust one' as the psalmist's oppressor (parallel to 'wicked' and 'ruthless'). The Piel intensifies deliberate moral perversity. Cross-linguistic glosses recognize both verbal ('acts unjustly') and nominal ('the unjust') uses.

gloss_terse: bird, fowl (Aramaic; collective or individual)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun denotes a bird or fowl, used in Daniel's apocalyptic visions. Daniel 2:38 interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream, declaring God has given him dominion over 'the birds of the sky' (along with beasts and humans). Daniel 7:6 describes the third beast with 'four wings of a fowl,' symbolizing swift conquest. The word is collective (birds in general) or singular (a bird), with context determining number. The imagery reinforces divine sovereignty over all creation and prophetic symbolism of earthly kingdoms.

senses.1: Bird or fowl in Aramaic, appearing in Daniel's visions. Daniel 2:38 lists 'birds of the sky' among creatures under Nebuchadnezzar's dominion; 7:6 describes a beast with 'wings of a fowl.' The term functions both collectively (birds) and individually (bird/fowl), emphasizing either divine sovereignty or symbolic representation of kingdoms.

gloss_terse: Ephai (personal name; ketiv: Ophai); a Netophathite leader post-fall of Jerusalem
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies a Netophathite (from Netophah near Bethlehem) who appears in Jeremiah 40:8 among the military leaders who came to Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC. The Masoretic text preserves two readings: the ketiv (written text) has 'Ophai' while the qere (read aloud) has 'Ephai.' This reflects scribal tradition and pronunciation variants. Ephai represents the Judean remnant seeking guidance in the chaotic aftermath of Babylonian conquest.

senses.1: A proper name for a Netophathite leader who joined Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall (Jeremiah 40:8). The name shows ketiv/qere variation (Ophai/Ephai), reflecting scribal pronunciation traditions. Both occurrences in the verse reflect this textual phenomenon. Greek versions (Iōphe, Ōphe, Ōphet) attempt to transliterate the uncertain pronunciation.
